entries.content:
Before anyone films a video, shoots an ad or draws the final pages of a comic, someone usually sketches the plan as a storyboard: one picture per shot, in order, with a short note about what happens and how long it lasts.

Most people already have those pictures. They are phone photos, screenshots, rough sketches or AI-generated frames sitting in a folder. What they don't have is a quick way to turn that folder into clean, numbered sheets they can print or send to a client.

In this tutorial, you'll build a browser-based tool that does exactly that. You'll add a set of images, give each one a title, a description and a duration, choose a layout, preview the sheets, and download a print-ready PDF.

Everything runs in the browser. The images are never uploaded to a server, which matters when the frames are unreleased product shots or client work.

Along the way, you'll learn how to fix sideways phone photos, sort files the way people expect, lay out a page in PDF points, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft with IndexedDB, and build a PDF that keeps photos sharp without making the file huge.

I built this tool for AllInOneTools, where it runs as the Image Storyboard to PDF tool. This article walks through a simplified version that you can build in three files.

What We'll Cover

What This Image Storyboard Tool Does and How It Works

The tool takes a list of images and turns them into storyboard sheets. Each image becomes a frame with:

  • a label, such as 
    Shot 1
    or 
    Scene 1
  • an optional title
  • a description of what happens
  • an optional duration in seconds

The frames are placed on sheets in one of four layouts:

  • One frame per page, for presenting each shot large
  • Grid, for seeing the whole sequence at a glance
  • Panels with notes, with ruled lines for handwritten notes on set
  • Film strip, with sprocket holes for a classic look

Each sheet has a title, the total running time and a sheet number at the top.

Here's the flow from start to finish:

Images → frames (title, description, duration)
       → layout (where each box goes, in PDF points)
       → canvas (labels, text, lines)
       → PDF (photos as JPEG + one text layer per sheet)
       → download

Why the Text Is Drawn on a Canvas

PDF-lib can write real text into a PDF, but only with a font file you embed. The standard PDF fonts only cover basic Latin characters, so a description in Hindi, Gujarati, Arabic or Japanese would fail.

A canvas, on the other hand, can draw any text the device can show, using the fonts the device already has. So this tool draws all the text on a canvas at 300 dpi and puts that canvas into the PDF as an image.

The trade-off is that the text in the PDF isn't selectable or searchable. For a storyboard, which is mostly printed and looked at, that's usually fine. If you need searchable text, you'd embed a font with PDF-lib's 

fontkit
support instead.

Project Setup

You need only three files:

image-storyboard/
├── index.html
├── style.css
└── script.js

Open 

index.html
through a local server (for example, the Live Server extension in VS Code) rather than as a 
file://
page, so that IndexedDB and downloads behave the same way they will on a real site.

Libraries and Browser APIs Used

This project uses one library and a few built-in browser APIs:

  • PDF-lib creates the PDF, embeds the JPEG and PNG images, and saves the file.
  • Canvas API draws the sheets for the preview and the text layer of the PDF.
  • createImageBitmap
    decodes images and applies the rotation stored in phone photos.
  • IndexedDB keeps a draft in the browser so the work survives a page reload.

You don't need PDF.js here, because there's no PDF to read. Everything starts from images.

Add PDF-lib with a pinned version at the end of the 

body
, before your own script:

Pinning the version means a future release of the library can't break your tool without you knowing.

Creating the HTML Layout

The page has four parts:

  • An upload area with a file input
  • A bar that offers to restore a saved draft
  • A frames panel with one card per image
  • A settings panel and a preview panel

Here's the upload area and the draft bar:




  
Drop images here or

The file input only accepts the formats every browser can decode: JPEG, PNG, WebP and GIF.

The workspace holds the three panels:




  

    

      
Frames

    The settings panel is a list of 

    select
    and 
    number
    inputs. Each one has an 
    id
    that matches a key in the settings object you'll create in JavaScript:
    
  
    Board settings

    The preview panel has the canvas, the sheet navigation and the download controls:

    
  
    Preview

    In 

    style.css
    , add one rule that's easy to forget:
    [hidden] { display: none !important; }

    The workspace uses 

    display: grid
    and the draft bar uses 
    display: flex
    . Those rules are more specific than the browser's default style for the 
    hidden
    attribute, so without this line, hidden elements would still show.

    Selecting the Main Elements

    At the top of 

    script.js
    , set up the constants, the state and the element references:
    // ---------- Constants ----------
const PAPERS = {
  a4: [595.28, 841.89],
  letter: [612, 792],
  a3: [841.89, 1190.55],
  slide: [405, 720],
};
const FONTS = {
  sans: "Arial, Helvetica, 'Noto Sans', sans-serif",
  serif: "Georgia, 'Times New Roman', 'Noto Serif', serif",
  mono: "'Courier New', Courier, monospace",
};
const THUMB_SIZE = 1000;
const ACCEPTED = ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp', 'image/gif'];

// ---------- State ----------
const state = {
  frames: [],
  title: '',
  sheet: 0,
  nextId: 1,
  lastDeleted: null,
  opts: {
    layout: 'grid', cols: 3, rows: 2, paper: 'a4', orient: 'landscape',
    label: 'shot', font: 'sans', textSize: 'm', lines: 3,
  },
};

// ---------- Elements ----------
const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const els = {
  uploadArea: $('uploadArea'), fileInput: $('fileInput'), selectBtn: $('selectBtn'),
  statusText: $('statusText'), workspace: $('workspace'), frameList: $('frameList'),
  totalTime: $('totalTime'), boardTitle: $('boardTitle'), undoBtn: $('undoBtn'),
  addMoreBtn: $('addMoreBtn'), canvas: $('previewCanvas'), prevBtn: $('prevBtn'),
  nextBtn: $('nextBtn'), sheetInfo: $('sheetInfo'), fileName: $('fileName'),
  quality: $('quality'), downloadBtn: $('downloadBtn'), resetBtn: $('resetBtn'),
  resultText: $('resultText'), draftBar: $('draftBar'), draftText: $('draftText'),
  restoreBtn: $('restoreBtn'), discardBtn: $('discardBtn'),
};
const SETTING_IDS = ['layout', 'cols', 'rows', 'paper', 'orient', 'label', 'font', 'textSize', 'lines'];

    The 

    state
    object is the single source of truth. The frame list, the preview and the PDF are all built from it, which keeps them in sync.

    The paper sizes are in PDF points. One point is 1/72 of an inch, so an A4 page is 595.28 × 841.89 points. You'll do all layout math in points and only convert to pixels when drawing.

    Adding and Loading Images

    Opening Files from the Button or by Dropping Them

    The "Select images" button opens the hidden file input, and dropping files anywhere on the page adds them too:

    // ---------- Upload area ----------
els.selectBtn.addEventListener('click', () => els.fileInput.click());
els.addMoreBtn.addEventListener('click', () => els.fileInput.click());
els.fileInput.addEventListener('change', () => {
  addFiles(els.fileInput.files);
  els.fileInput.value = '';
});

['dragenter', 'dragover'].forEach((type) => {
  document.addEventListener(type, (e) => {
    if (!e.dataTransfer.types.includes('Files')) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    els.uploadArea.classList.add('dragover');
  });
});
['dragleave', 'drop'].forEach((type) => {
  document.addEventListener(type, () => els.uploadArea.classList.remove('dragover'));
});
document.addEventListener('drop', (e) => {
  if (!e.dataTransfer.files.length) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  addFiles(e.dataTransfer.files);
});

function showWorkspace() {
  els.uploadArea.hidden = true;
  els.draftBar.hidden = true;
  els.workspace.hidden = false;
}

    Resetting 

    fileInput.value
    after each pick lets the user choose the same file again later. The 
    dataTransfer.types.includes('Files')
    check makes sure the drop highlight only appears for files, not for frames being dragged inside the list.

    Fixing Phone Photo Rotation

    Phones don't rotate the pixels when you hold them sideways. They save the image in the sensor's orientation and add an EXIF tag that says "rotate this 90° when you show it."

    If you draw such a photo on a canvas with an 

    img
    element in some browsers, or read its width and height before the rotation is applied, the frame comes out sideways or with the wrong shape.

    createImageBitmap
    with 
    imageOrientation: 'from-image'
    asks the browser to apply the EXIF rotation while decoding:
    // ---------- Loading images ----------
// Phone photos store their rotation in EXIF. imageOrientation: 'from-image'
// asks the browser to apply it, so the picture comes out the right way up.
function decodeImage(blob) {
  if ('createImageBitmap' in window) {
    return createImageBitmap(blob, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' })
      .catch(() => loadWithImgTag(blob));
  }
  return loadWithImgTag(blob);
}

function loadWithImgTag(blob) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
    const img = new Image();
    img.onload = () => { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); resolve(img); };
    img.onerror = () => { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); reject(new Error('decode')); };
    img.src = url;
  });
}

function canvasToBlob(canvas, type, quality) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    canvas.toBlob((b) => (b ? resolve(b) : reject(new Error('encode'))), type, quality);
  });
}

    If 

    createImageBitmap
    isn't available or fails, the code falls back to a normal 
    img
    element. Modern browsers apply EXIF rotation to 
    img
    elements by default too.

    canvasToBlob
    wraps the callback-based 
    canvas.toBlob()
    in a Promise, so you can use it with 
    await
    .

    Making a Frame Object with a Thumbnail

    A phone photo can be 4000 × 3000 pixels or more. Drawing dozens of those every time the user types a letter would make the preview slow.

    So each frame keeps the original file for the PDF, plus a small JPEG copy (at most 1000 pixels on its longest side) for the frame list and the preview:

    async function makeFrame(file) {
  const pic = await decodeImage(file);
  const w = pic.naturalWidth || pic.width;
  const h = pic.naturalHeight || pic.height;

  // A small copy for the frame list and the preview
  const scale = Math.min(1, THUMB_SIZE / Math.max(w, h));
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = Math.round(w * scale);
  c.height = Math.round(h * scale);
  const ctx = c.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  ctx.drawImage(pic, 0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  if (pic.close) pic.close();

  const thumb = await canvasToBlob(c, 'image/jpeg', 0.86);
  return {
    id: 'f' + state.nextId++,
    blob: file, name: file.name, w, h,
    thumb, thumbUrl: URL.createObjectURL(thumb), thumbPic: null,
    title: '', desc: '', dur: '',
  };
}

    Notice that 

    w
    and 
    h
    are read after decoding, so they're the size after rotation. A portrait phone photo gets a portrait frame.

    The white fill before drawing matters for PNG images with transparency. JPEG has no transparency, so transparent areas would otherwise turn black.

    Sorting by File Name

    People name their files 

    shot-1.jpg
    , 
    shot-2.jpg
    … 
    shot-10.jpg
    . A normal string sort puts 
    shot-10
    before 
    shot-2
    , because it compares the character 
    1
    with 
    2
    .

    localeCompare
    with the 
    numeric
    option compares the numbers inside the names as numbers:
    // "shot-2.jpg" before "shot-10.jpg"
function naturalCompare(a, b) {
  return a.localeCompare(b, undefined, { numeric: true, sensitivity: 'base' });
}

    Adding the Files

    addFiles
    filters out unsupported files, sorts the rest, turns each into a frame and reports anything it skipped:
    async function addFiles(fileList) {
  const files = Array.from(fileList);
  const images = files.filter((f) => ACCEPTED.includes(f.type))
    .sort((a, b) => naturalCompare(a.name, b.name));
  const skipped = files.length - images.length;
  let failed = 0;

  for (let i = 0; i < images.length; i++) {
    els.statusText.textContent = `Reading image ${i + 1} of ${images.length}...`;
    try {
      state.frames.push(await makeFrame(images[i]));
    } catch (err) {
      failed++;
    }
  }

  const notes = [];
  if (skipped) notes.push(`${skipped} file(s) skipped: not JPG, PNG, WebP or GIF`);
  if (failed) notes.push(`${failed} image(s) couldn't be read`);
  els.statusText.textContent = notes.join('. ');

  if (state.frames.length) {
    showWorkspace();
    renderFrameList();
    drawPreview();
    saveDraftSoon();
  }
}

    The images are read one at a time, not all at once with 

    Promise.all
    . Decoding 50 large photos in parallel can run a phone out of memory, and reading them in order also keeps the status message accurate.

    Managing the Frames

    The Frame Card

    Each frame gets a card with its thumbnail, a title field, a description box, a duration field and three buttons:

    // ---------- Frame list ----------
function escapeHtml(s) {
  const map = { '&': '&', '<': '<', '>': '>', '"': '"', "'": ''' };
  return String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) => map[c]);
}

function renderFrameList() {
  els.frameList.innerHTML = state.frames.map((f, i) => `
    
  1. 
      
      
    
        ${i + 1}. ${escapeHtml(f.name)}
        
        
        
        
    
          
          
          
        
    
      
    
    
    2. `).join('');
  updateTotal();
}

function updateTotal() {
  const total = totalDuration();
  els.totalTime.textContent = `${state.frames.length} frames` + (total ? `, ${formatDuration(total)}` : '');
}

function findFrame(el) {
  const li = el.closest('[data-id]');
  return li ? state.frames.findIndex((f) => f.id === li.dataset.id) : -1;
}

    Titles and descriptions come from the user, so they're escaped before going into the HTML. Without 

    escapeHtml
    , a title like 
    Shot "A"
    would break the 
    value
    attribute.

    Updating the State While Typing

    If you rebuilt the whole list on every key press, the text field would lose focus after each letter. Instead, one 

    input
    listener on the list updates only the state:
    els.frameList.addEventListener('input', (e) => {
  const i = findFrame(e.target);
  const field = e.target.dataset.field;
  if (i < 0 || !field) return;
  state.frames[i][field] = e.target.value;
  updateTotal();
  drawPreviewSoon();
  saveDraftSoon();
});

    This uses event delegation: one listener on the list handles every field in every card, including cards added later. The 

    data-field
    attribute tells it which property to update.

    The preview redraw is delayed with 

    drawPreviewSoon()
    , which you'll write later, so it runs once when the user pauses typing rather than on every letter.

    Durations and the Total Running Time

    Durations are stored in seconds and shown as 

    4.5 s
    under a minute or 
    1:10
    from one minute up:
    // ---------- Durations ----------
function formatDuration(seconds) {
  const s = Number(seconds) || 0;
  if (s <= 0) return '';
  if (s < 60) return `${Math.round(s * 10) / 10} s`;
  const m = Math.floor(s / 60);
  const r = Math.round(s - m * 60);
  return `${m}:${String(r).padStart(2, '0')}`;
}

function totalDuration() {
  return state.frames.reduce((sum, f) => sum + (Number(f.dur) || 0), 0);
}

    Reordering Frames

    The Up and Down buttons, and the Delete button, are handled by one click listener:

    els.frameList.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('[data-act]');
  if (!btn) return;
  const i = findFrame(btn);
  if (btn.dataset.act === 'up') moveFrame(i, i - 1);
  if (btn.dataset.act === 'down') moveFrame(i, i + 1);
  if (btn.dataset.act === 'delete') deleteFrame(i);
});

function moveFrame(from, to) {
  if (to < 0 || to >= state.frames.length || from === to) return;
  const [frame] = state.frames.splice(from, 1);
  state.frames.splice(to, 0, frame);
  renderFrameList();
  drawPreview();
  saveDraftSoon();
}


    splice(from, 1)
    removes the frame, and 
    splice(to, 0, frame)
    puts it back at its new position.

    For mouse users, dragging a thumbnail onto another card moves it there. The HTML5 drag and drop API needs 

    preventDefault()
    in 
    dragover
    , or the browser won't allow the drop:
    // Drag a thumbnail onto another card to move it there
let dragIndex = -1;
els.frameList.addEventListener('dragstart', (e) => {
  dragIndex = findFrame(e.target);
  e.dataTransfer.effectAllowed = 'move';
  e.target.closest('li').classList.add('dragging');
});
els.frameList.addEventListener('dragover', (e) => {
  if (dragIndex > -1) e.preventDefault();
});
els.frameList.addEventListener('drop', (e) => {
  if (dragIndex < 0) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  e.stopPropagation();
  const to = findFrame(e.target);
  moveFrame(dragIndex, to < 0 ? state.frames.length - 1 : to);
  dragIndex = -1;
});
els.frameList.addEventListener('dragend', () => {
  dragIndex = -1;
  els.frameList.querySelectorAll('.dragging').forEach((li) => li.classList.remove('dragging'));
});


    stopPropagation()
    in the 
    drop
    handler stops the document-level drop handler from treating the move as a new file drop.

    Keep the Up and Down buttons even with drag and drop. Drag and drop doesn't work with a keyboard, and it's awkward on touch screens.

    Deleting a Frame with Undo

    Deleting a frame that has a long description typed into it is painful if it was a mistake. So the tool keeps the last deleted frame and its position:

    function deleteFrame(i) {
  const [frame] = state.frames.splice(i, 1);
  state.lastDeleted = { frame, index: i };
  els.undoBtn.hidden = false;
  renderFrameList();
  drawPreview();
  saveDraftSoon();
}

els.undoBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  if (!state.lastDeleted) return;
  const { frame, index } = state.lastDeleted;
  state.frames.splice(Math.min(index, state.frames.length), 0, frame);
  state.lastDeleted = null;
  els.undoBtn.hidden = true;
  renderFrameList();
  drawPreview();
  saveDraftSoon();
});


    Math.min(index, state.frames.length)
    puts the frame back at the end if the list got shorter in the meantime.

    Building the Board Settings

    All settings are read into 

    state.opts
    in one place, with the number fields limited to a sensible range:
    // ---------- Settings ----------
function readSettings() {
  const o = state.opts;
  SETTING_IDS.forEach((id) => { o[id] = $(id).value; });
  o.cols = Math.min(6, Math.max(1, parseInt(o.cols, 10) || 1));
  o.rows = Math.min(6, Math.max(1, parseInt(o.rows, 10) || 1));
  o.lines = Math.min(6, Math.max(1, parseInt(o.lines, 10) || 1));
}

SETTING_IDS.forEach((id) => {
  $(id).addEventListener('change', () => {
    readSettings();
    state.sheet = 0;
    drawPreview();
  });
});

els.boardTitle.addEventListener('input', () => {
  state.title = els.boardTitle.value.trim();
  drawPreviewSoon();
  saveDraftSoon();
});

    Any change goes back to the first sheet and redraws the preview. The board title is saved as a draft too, because it's part of the user's work.

    The four layouts change only the arrangement. The frame data stays the same, so users can switch layouts freely without losing anything.

    Laying Out a Storyboard Sheet

    This is the heart of the tool. Before drawing anything, the code works out where every box goes, in PDF points from the top-left corner of the sheet.

    Keeping layout separate from drawing means the same layout is used for the small preview on screen and for the 300 dpi PDF. They can't drift apart.

    Calculating the Sheet Size

    // ---------- Layout: where everything goes, in PDF points from the top-left ----------
function sheetSize(o) {
  const [a, b] = PAPERS[o.paper];
  const short = Math.min(a, b);
  const long = Math.max(a, b);
  return o.orient === 'portrait' ? [short, long] : [long, short];
}

    The paper sizes are stored once. Landscape just swaps the short and long sides.

    Laying Out the Frame Boxes

    function computeLayout(o, frameCount) {
  const [W, H] = sheetSize(o);
  const short = Math.min(W, H);
  const margin = short * 0.05;
  const gap = 10;
  const cols = o.layout === 'page' ? 1 : o.cols;
  const rows = o.layout === 'page' ? 1 : o.rows;
  const perSheet = cols * rows;
  const sheets = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(frameCount / perSheet));

  const headH = short * 0.045;              // the title row at the top of each sheet
  const top = margin + headH + margin * 0.5;
  const box = { x: margin, y: top, w: W - 2 * margin, h: H - top - margin };
  const sizeScale = { s: 0.85, m: 1, l: 1.2 }[o.textSize];

  const cellW = (box.w - (cols - 1) * gap) / cols;
  const cellH = (box.h - (rows - 1) * gap) / rows;
  const cells = [];

  for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
    for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
      const x = box.x + c * (cellW + gap);
      const y = box.y + r * (cellH + gap);
      const fs = Math.min(13, Math.max(6.5, cellW * 0.05)) * sizeScale;
      const lh = fs * 1.3;

      if (o.layout === 'notes') {
        // picture on the left, title and ruled lines on the right
        const imgW = Math.min(cellW * 0.5, cellH * 1.6);
        const tx = x + imgW + 8;
        cells.push({ img: { x, y, w: imgW, h: cellH }, text: { x: tx, y, w: x + cellW - tx, h: cellH }, fs, lh, notes: true });
      } else {
        // picture on top, text underneath
        const textH = lh * (1.2 + Number(o.lines)) + fs * 0.6;
        const imgH = Math.max(10, cellH - textH);
        cells.push({ img: { x, y, w: cellW, h: imgH }, text: { x, y: y + imgH + fs * 0.6, w: cellW, h: textH - fs * 0.6 }, fs, lh, strip: o.layout === 'strip' });
      }
    }
  }
  return { W, H, margin, headH, perSheet, sheets, cells };
}

    Here's what happens step by step:

    • The margin is 
      5%
      of the short side, so it scales with the paper.
    • The "One frame per page" layout is a 1 × 1 grid.
    • The number of sheets is the number of frames divided by the frames per sheet, rounded up.
    • A row at the top is kept for the sheet heading.
    • The remaining box is split into equal cells with a fixed gap.
    • The font size depends on the cell width (
      5%
      of it), kept between 
      6.5
      and 
      13
      points, then scaled by the Text size setting.
    • In most layouts, the picture sits on top and the text underneath. The text area is sized for the label line plus the chosen number of description lines.
    • In "Panels with notes", the picture is on the left and the text and ruled lines on the right.

    Each cell ends up with an 

    img
    box and a 
    text
    box, and that's all the drawing code needs to know.

    Fitting an Image Without Stretching It

    A cell is rarely the same shape as the picture. Stretching would distort faces and products, and cropping might cut off what matters. So the picture is scaled to fit inside the box, keeping its proportions, and centered:

    function fitContain(imgW, imgH, box) {
  const s = Math.min(box.w / imgW, box.h / imgH);
  const w = imgW * s;
  const h = imgH * s;
  return { x: box.x + (box.w - w) / 2, y: box.y + (box.h - h) / 2, w, h };
}

    This is the same idea as 

    object-fit: contain
    in CSS. The smaller of the two scale factors wins, so the whole picture always fits.

    Drawing a Sheet on the Canvas

    Wrapping Text into Lines

    Canvas has no automatic line wrapping. 

    fillText
    draws one line, however long it is. So you measure words with 
    measureText
    and build the lines yourself:
    // ---------- Text ----------
function wrapText(ctx, text, maxWidth, maxLines) {
  const words = String(text).trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  const lines = [];
  let line = '';
  for (const word of words) {
    const test = line ? line + ' ' + word : word;
    if (ctx.measureText(test).width <= maxWidth || !line) {
      line = test;
    } else {
      lines.push(line);
      line = word;
    }
  }
  if (line) lines.push(line);

  if (lines.length > maxLines) {
    lines.length = maxLines;
    let last = lines[maxLines - 1];
    while (last && ctx.measureText(last + '…').width > maxWidth) last = last.slice(0, -1);
    lines[maxLines - 1] = last.trimEnd() + '…';
  }
  return lines;
}

    If the description is longer than the lines available, the last line ends with an ellipsis, so the user can see that text was cut.

    Drawing Labels, Titles and Durations

    function frameLabel(o, index) {
  if (o.label === 'number') return String(index + 1);
  if (o.label === 'scene') return `Scene ${index + 1}`;
  if (o.label === 'shot') return `Shot ${index + 1}`;
  return '';
}

function drawFrameText(ctx, o, cell, frame, index, k) {
  const fs = cell.fs * k;
  const lh = cell.lh * k;
  const x = cell.text.x * k;
  const w = cell.text.w * k;
  let y = cell.text.y * k + fs;

  ctx.fillStyle = '#16181b';
  ctx.textBaseline = 'alphabetic';

  // Line 1: label and title on the left, duration on the right
  const dur = formatDuration(frame.dur);
  let room = w;
  if (dur) {
    ctx.font = `${fs}px ${FONTS.mono}`;
    ctx.textAlign = 'right';
    ctx.fillText(dur, x + w, y);
    room -= ctx.measureText(dur).width + fs;
  }
  ctx.textAlign = 'left';
  const head = [frameLabel(o, index), frame.title.trim()].filter(Boolean).join('  ');
  if (head) {
    ctx.font = `bold ${fs}px ${FONTS[o.font]}`;
    ctx.fillText(wrapText(ctx, head, room, 1)[0] || '', x, y);
  }
  y += lh * 1.2;

  // Description, wrapped and cut to the chosen number of lines
  ctx.font = `${fs}px ${FONTS[o.font]}`;
  const maxLines = cell.notes ? Math.floor((cell.text.h * k - lh * 1.2) / lh) : Number(o.lines);
  const lines = frame.desc.trim() ? wrapText(ctx, frame.desc, w, maxLines) : [];
  lines.forEach((line, j) => ctx.fillText(line, x, y + j * lh));

  // Ruled lines for handwritten notes
  if (cell.notes) {
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#c9c6bd';
    ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, 0.6 * k);
    const bottom = (cell.text.y + cell.text.h) * k;
    for (let ly = y + lines.length * lh; ly < bottom - 2; ly += lh * 1.25) {
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(x, ly);
      ctx.lineTo(x + w, ly);
      ctx.stroke();
    }
  }
}

    The parameter 

    k
    is the scale from points to pixels. All positions come from the layout in points and are multiplied by 
    k
    just before drawing. That's what lets the same function draw a 600-pixel preview and a 300 dpi PDF page.

    The duration is drawn first, right-aligned, and the space it takes is subtracted from the room left for the label and title. That way a long title never runs into the duration.

    Drawing the Whole Sheet

    drawSheet
    draws the heading, then each frame on the sheet:
    // ---------- Drawing one sheet ----------
// k turns PDF points into canvas pixels. With mode 'preview' the pictures are
// drawn too; with mode 'overlay' their boxes are left transparent for the PDF.
async function drawSheet(ctx, o, L, sheetIndex, k, mode) {
  const W = L.W * k;
  const H = L.H * k;
  const placed = [];

  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
  ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);

  // Sheet heading: title on the left, total time and sheet number on the right
  const headFs = L.headH * 0.6 * k;
  const base = (L.margin + L.headH * 0.78) * k;
  const total = totalDuration();
  const right = [total ? `Total ${formatDuration(total)}` : '', `Sheet ${sheetIndex + 1} of ${L.sheets}`].filter(Boolean).join(', ');
  ctx.font = `${headFs * 0.72}px ${FONTS.mono}`;
  ctx.fillStyle = '#55585e';
  ctx.textAlign = 'right';
  ctx.fillText(right, W - L.margin * k, base);
  if (state.title) {
    ctx.font = `bold ${headFs}px ${FONTS[o.font]}`;
    ctx.fillStyle = '#16181b';
    ctx.textAlign = 'left';
    ctx.fillText(state.title, L.margin * k, base);
  }
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#c9c6bd';
  ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, 0.75 * k);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(L.margin * k, (L.margin + L.headH) * k);
  ctx.lineTo(W - L.margin * k, (L.margin + L.headH) * k);
  ctx.stroke();

  const start = sheetIndex * L.perSheet;
  const items = state.frames.slice(start, start + L.perSheet);

  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    const cell = L.cells[i];
    const frame = items[i];

    // Film strip: a dark band with sprocket holes behind the picture
    if (cell.strip) {
      const b = cell.img;
      const hole = b.h * 0.08;
      ctx.fillStyle = '#16181b';
      ctx.fillRect(b.x * k, b.y * k, b.w * k, b.h * k);
      ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
      for (let hx = b.x + hole; hx + hole < b.x + b.w; hx += hole * 2) {
        ctx.fillRect(hx * k, (b.y + hole * 0.3) * k, hole * k, hole * 0.5 * k);
        ctx.fillRect(hx * k, (b.y + b.h - hole * 0.8) * k, hole * k, hole * 0.5 * k);
      }
    }

    const area = cell.strip
      ? { x: cell.img.x, y: cell.img.y + cell.img.h * 0.12, w: cell.img.w, h: cell.img.h * 0.76 }
      : cell.img;
    const rect = fitContain(frame.w, frame.h, area);
    placed.push({ frame, rect });

    const px = { x: Math.round(rect.x * k), y: Math.round(rect.y * k), w: Math.round(rect.w * k), h: Math.round(rect.h * k) };
    if (mode === 'overlay') {
      ctx.clearRect(px.x, px.y, px.w, px.h);
    } else {
      if (!frame.thumbPic) frame.thumbPic = await decodeImage(frame.thumb);
      ctx.drawImage(frame.thumbPic, px.x, px.y, px.w, px.h);
    }
    if (!cell.strip) {
      ctx.strokeStyle = '#16181b';
      ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(1, 0.9 * k);
      ctx.strokeRect(cell.img.x * k, cell.img.y * k, cell.img.w * k, cell.img.h * k);
    }
    drawFrameText(ctx, o, cell, frame, start + i, k);
  }
  return placed;
}

    The 

    mode
    parameter is the important trick here:
    • In 
      'preview'
      mode, the pictures are drawn from the thumbnails.
    • In 
      'overlay'
      mode, the picture areas are cleared to transparent, and the function returns where each picture should go.

    You'll see why in the PDF section. For the film strip, the dark band and the sprocket holes are drawn first, and the picture sits in the middle of the band.

    Previewing the Sheets

    The preview draws the current sheet at the canvas's on-screen width, multiplied by the device pixel ratio so it stays sharp on high-density screens:

    // ---------- Preview ----------
let previewTimer = null;
function drawPreviewSoon() {
  clearTimeout(previewTimer);
  previewTimer = setTimeout(drawPreview, 150);
}

async function drawPreview() {
  if (!state.frames.length) return;
  const o = state.opts;
  const L = computeLayout(o, state.frames.length);
  state.sheet = Math.min(state.sheet, L.sheets - 1);

  // Draw at the canvas's on-screen width, sharp on high-density screens
  const cssWidth = els.canvas.clientWidth || 600;
  const k = (cssWidth * Math.min(2, window.devicePixelRatio || 1)) / L.W;
  els.canvas.width = Math.round(L.W * k);
  els.canvas.height = Math.round(L.H * k);
  await drawSheet(els.canvas.getContext('2d'), o, L, state.sheet, k, 'preview');

  els.sheetInfo.textContent = `Sheet ${state.sheet + 1} of ${L.sheets}`;
  els.prevBtn.disabled = state.sheet === 0;
  els.nextBtn.disabled = state.sheet >= L.sheets - 1;
}

els.prevBtn.addEventListener('click', () => { state.sheet--; drawPreview(); });
els.nextBtn.addEventListener('click', () => { state.sheet++; drawPreview(); });

    The device pixel ratio is capped at 2. A 3× phone screen would otherwise create a canvas nine times the size of the CSS box, which is slow and adds little you can see.

    Saving a Draft with IndexedDB

    Writing descriptions for 30 frames takes time. Losing that work to an accidental reload is frustrating, so the tool saves a draft as the user works.

    localStorage
    won't do here. It only stores strings, and most browsers limit it to about 5 MB, which is less than two phone photos. IndexedDB can store 
    Blob
    objects directly and allows far more space.

    Opening the Database

    // ---------- Draft in IndexedDB ----------
const DB_NAME = 'image-storyboard';
let dbPromise = null;

function openDb() {
  if (!dbPromise) {
    dbPromise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const req = indexedDB.open(DB_NAME, 1);
      req.onupgradeneeded = () => req.result.createObjectStore('drafts');
      req.onsuccess = () => resolve(req.result);
      req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
    });
  }
  return dbPromise;
}

async function dbRun(mode, work) {
  const db = await openDb();
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const tx = db.transaction('drafts', mode);
    const result = work(tx.objectStore('drafts'));
    tx.oncomplete = () => resolve(result && result.result);
    tx.onerror = () => reject(tx.error);
  });
}


    dbRun
    wraps a transaction in a Promise. It resolves when the transaction completes, so a write is only reported as done once it's actually stored.

    Saving the Draft

    let saveTimer = null;
function saveDraftSoon() {
  clearTimeout(saveTimer);
  saveTimer = setTimeout(saveDraft, 800);
}

function saveDraft() {
  const draft = {
    title: state.title,
    savedAt: Date.now(),
    frames: state.frames.map(({ blob, name, title, desc, dur }) => ({ blob, name, title, desc, dur })),
  };
  return dbRun('readwrite', (store) => store.put(draft, 'current')).catch(() => {
    els.resultText.textContent = 'This browser could not save a draft. Download the PDF before closing the tab.';
  });
}

    The draft stores the original image files as Blobs, along with the text the user typed. Thumbnails and object URLs aren't stored, because they can be made again from the files.

    saveDraftSoon
    waits until the user pauses for 800 ms, so typing a description doesn't write to the database on every key press.

    If saving fails, for example in a private window with storage blocked, the tool tells the user to download the PDF before closing the tab instead of failing silently.

    Restoring the Draft

    When the page loads, the tool checks for a draft and offers to restore it:

    async function checkDraft() {
  try {
    const draft = await dbRun('readonly', (store) => store.get('current'));
    if (!draft || !draft.frames.length) return;
    els.draftText.textContent = `You have a saved storyboard with ${draft.frames.length} frames.`;
    els.draftBar.hidden = false;
  } catch (err) { /* no storage: nothing to restore */ }
}

els.restoreBtn.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const draft = await dbRun('readonly', (store) => store.get('current'));
  for (const saved of draft.frames) {
    const file = new File([saved.blob], saved.name, { type: saved.blob.type });
    const frame = await makeFrame(file);
    Object.assign(frame, { title: saved.title, desc: saved.desc, dur: saved.dur });
    state.frames.push(frame);
  }
  state.title = draft.title || '';
  els.boardTitle.value = state.title;
  showWorkspace();
  renderFrameList();
  drawPreview();
});

els.discardBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  dbRun('readwrite', (store) => store.delete('current'));
  els.draftBar.hidden = true;
});

    Each saved Blob goes back through 

    makeFrame
    , so restored frames get fresh thumbnails, and then the saved text is copied onto them.

    Generating the PDF with PDF-lib

    The simplest way to make the PDF would be to draw each whole sheet on a canvas, with the pictures, and put that canvas in the PDF as one image. It works, but it forces a choice:

    • Save it as PNG and the photos make the file huge.
    • Save it as JPEG and the text and thin lines get blurry edges.

    So the tool uses two layers on each page:

    • Pictures as JPEG, each at the resolution the user chose, placed exactly in its box
    • Text, labels and lines as one transparent PNG at 300 dpi, covering the whole page on top

    JPEG is good for photos, and PNG keeps text sharp. This is why 

    drawSheet
    has the 
    'overlay'
    mode that leaves holes where the pictures go.

    Turning Each Picture into a JPEG

    // ---------- Making the PDF ----------
async function imageAsJpeg(frame, widthPx, heightPx) {
  const pic = await decodeImage(frame.blob);
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = Math.max(1, Math.round(widthPx));
  c.height = Math.max(1, Math.round(heightPx));
  const ctx = c.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';              // transparent PNGs get a white background
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  ctx.imageSmoothingQuality = 'high';
  ctx.drawImage(pic, 0, 0, c.width, c.height);
  if (pic.close) pic.close();
  const blob = await canvasToBlob(c, 'image/jpeg', 0.9);
  return new Uint8Array(await blob.arrayBuffer());
}

    The picture is decoded again from the original file, not from the thumbnail, so the PDF has full quality.

    Building the Pages

    async function buildPdf() {
  const { PDFDocument } = PDFLib;
  const o = state.opts;
  const L = computeLayout(o, state.frames.length);
  const dpi = Number(els.quality.value);
  const k = 300 / 72;                         // text layer at 300 dpi

  const pdf = await PDFDocument.create();
  for (let s = 0; s < L.sheets; s++) {
    els.resultText.textContent = `Making sheet ${s + 1} of ${L.sheets}...`;
    const page = pdf.addPage([L.W, L.H]);

    // 1. Text, labels and lines on a canvas, with holes where the pictures go
    const c = document.createElement('canvas');
    c.width = Math.round(L.W * k);
    c.height = Math.round(L.H * k);
    const placed = await drawSheet(c.getContext('2d'), o, L, s, k, 'overlay');

    // 2. Each picture as a JPEG at the chosen resolution, placed in its hole
    for (const { frame, rect } of placed) {
      const scale = Math.min(1, (rect.w * dpi / 72) / frame.w);
      const jpg = await pdf.embedJpg(await imageAsJpeg(frame, frame.w * scale, frame.h * scale));
      // PDF y runs from the bottom of the page, the canvas y from the top
      page.drawImage(jpg, { x: rect.x, y: L.H - rect.y - rect.h, width: rect.w, height: rect.h });
    }

    // 3. The text layer on top, as one transparent PNG covering the page
    const pngBlob = await canvasToBlob(c, 'image/png');
    const png = await pdf.embedPng(new Uint8Array(await pngBlob.arrayBuffer()));
    page.drawImage(png, { x: 0, y: 0, width: L.W, height: L.H });
    c.width = 1;                               // free the canvas memory
  }

  pdf.setTitle(state.title || 'Storyboard');
  return pdf.save();
}

    Here's what happens on each page:

    • addPage([L.W, L.H])
      creates a page in points, the same units as the layout.
    • The text layer is drawn at 
      k = 300 / 72
      , which is 300 pixels per inch.
    • Each picture is resized to the chosen dpi for the size it has on the page. A 4000-pixel photo shown 2 inches wide only needs 600 pixels at 300 dpi, so the file stays small. 
      Math.min(1, ...)
      makes sure small pictures are never enlarged.
    • The pictures are drawn first, then the transparent PNG on top of them.

    Note the y coordinate: 

    L.H - rect.y - rect.h
    . The layout and the canvas measure y from the top of the page, but PDF measures y from the bottom. Forgetting this flip puts every picture upside down in the page, the classic PDF-lib mistake.

    Setting 

    c.width = 1
    after use frees the canvas memory right away, which matters on phones when there are many sheets.

    Renaming and Downloading

    The file name comes from a text field, cleaned of characters that aren't allowed in file names:

    // ---------- Download ----------
function cleanFileName(name) {
  const n = name.trim().replace(/\.pdf$/i, '').replace(/[\\/:*?"<>|]+/g, '-');
  return (n || 'storyboard') + '.pdf';
}

function formatSize(bytes) {
  return bytes < 1024 * 1024 ? `${Math.round(bytes / 1024)} KB` : `${(bytes / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(1)} MB`;
}

els.downloadBtn.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  if (!state.frames.length) return;
  els.downloadBtn.disabled = true;
  try {
    const bytes = await buildPdf();
    const name = cleanFileName(els.fileName.value);
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([bytes], { type: 'application/pdf' }));
    const a = document.createElement('a');
    a.href = url;
    a.download = name;
    a.click();
    setTimeout(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(url), 60000);
    els.resultText.textContent = `Saved ${name} (${formatSize(bytes.length)}).`;
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err);
    els.resultText.textContent = 'The PDF could not be made. Try fewer images or the 150 dpi setting.';
  } finally {
    els.downloadBtn.disabled = false;
  }
});

    The object URL is revoked after a minute, which is long enough for the download to start and frees the memory afterwards. The button is disabled while the PDF is being made, so a double click can't start two exports.

    Finally, "Start over" clears the state, the draft and the object URLs. The last two lines of the file read the default settings and check for a saved draft when the page loads:

    // ---------- Start over ----------
els.resetBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  clearTimeout(saveTimer);
  state.frames.forEach((f) => URL.revokeObjectURL(f.thumbUrl));
  state.frames = [];
  state.title = '';
  state.sheet = 0;
  state.lastDeleted = null;
  els.boardTitle.value = '';
  els.undoBtn.hidden = true;
  els.resultText.textContent = '';
  els.workspace.hidden = true;
  els.uploadArea.hidden = false;
  dbRun('readwrite', (store) => store.delete('current')).catch(() => {});
});

readSettings();
checkDraft();

    Demo: How the Image Storyboard Tool Works

    Here's the whole workflow in the finished tool.

    Step 1: Add Your Images

    Drop a folder's worth of images on the page or click Select images. They're sorted by file name, so 

    shot-1
    , 
    shot-2
    … 
    shot-10
    land in the right order.

    Step 2: Put the Frames in Order

    Drag a thumbnail onto another card, or use the Up and Down buttons.

    Step 3: Write the Script

    Give each frame a title, a description and a duration. The total running time updates as you type.

    Step 4: Choose a Layout

    Pick one frame per page, a grid, panels with notes or a film strip, then set the paper size and orientation.

    Step 5: Check the Preview

    Use Previous and Next to look at every sheet before you download.

    Step 6: Download the PDF

    Type a file name, choose the image quality and click Download PDF.

    Performance Tips

    Use thumbnails for everything on screen. The preview redraws often, while the user types and changes settings. Drawing 1000-pixel thumbnails instead of full photos keeps it fast. Only the PDF export touches the original files.

    Decode thumbnails once. In 

    drawSheet
    , each frame keeps its decoded thumbnail in 
    frame.thumbPic
    , so switching sheets doesn't decode the same image again.

    Process images one at a time. Reading or exporting dozens of large photos with 

    Promise.all
    can use more memory than a phone has. A simple 
    for
    loop with 
    await
    keeps only one large image in memory at a time.

    Size pictures for the page, not the camera. A picture's pixel size in the PDF should depend on how big it is on the page and the chosen dpi. That one line in 

    buildPdf
    is often the difference between a 3 MB file and a 60 MB file.

    Release memory as you go. Call 

    close()
    on an 
    ImageBitmap
    when you're done with it, set used canvases to 
    width = 1
    , and revoke object URLs you no longer need.

    Common Mistakes

    Sideways phone photos. If you read an image's size or draw it without applying EXIF orientation, portrait photos come out landscape. Use 

    createImageBitmap(blob, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' })
    .

    Stretched pictures. Drawing an image straight into a cell with 

    drawImage(img, x, y, cellW, cellH)
    stretches it. Always fit it with a "contain" calculation like 
    fitContain
    first.

    Wrong order of files. The order files arrive from a file picker or a drop isn't guaranteed. Sort them yourself, and use a numeric sort so 

    shot-10
    comes after 
    shot-9
    .

    Forgetting to flip the y axis. Canvas y goes down from the top, PDF y goes up from the bottom. Convert with 

    pageHeight - y - height
    when placing anything with PDF-lib.

    Black backgrounds on transparent PNGs. JPEG has no transparency. Fill the canvas with white before drawing a PNG you'll save as JPEG.

    Rebuilding the list while the user types. Re-rendering inputs on every key press moves the cursor and loses focus. Update the state from the 

    input
    event and only rebuild the list when the order changes.

    Canvases that are too large. Browsers limit canvas size, and phones have tight limits. An A3 page at 300 dpi is about 4960 × 3508 pixels, which is fine, but don't multiply that by the device pixel ratio as well.

    Conclusion

    In this tutorial, you built a browser-based tool that turns a set of images into storyboard sheets and a print-ready PDF.

    You learned how to apply phone photo rotation with 

    createImageBitmap
    , sort file names numerically, keep layout math in PDF points so the preview and the PDF always match, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft of images and text in IndexedDB, and build a two-layer PDF with sharp text and compact photos using PDF-lib.

    All of it runs locally in the browser, so the images stay on the user's device.

    You can try the full version of this tool, with more options such as sheet colors, a handwritten font, one PDF per frame and PNG export, at Image Storyboard to PDF.

entries.content:
AI coding agents such as Codex read your codebase, edit multiple files, and run commands and tests while they work through larger tasks with you. In Codex, an AGENTS.md file holds persistent instructions for a project, and config.toml holds the agent's configuration.

We just published a course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you how to get reliable results from a coding agent by giving it the right context, planning the work, controlling its permissions, and verifying every change. This course is taught by Tom Chant, Head of Education at Scrimba.

You'll work through realistic tasks, including challenges on skills, characterization tests, and config.toml. The course is aimed at experienced developers adding AI to their workflow and at non-coders who want to build software with AI help. You can also study it interactively on Scrimba.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Prompting & Project Setup

    How to write effective prompts and comment prompts for a coding agent, then initialize a project and use multiple AGENTS.md files.
  • Plan Mode & Skills

    How to break larger development tasks down with Plan Mode and extend a coding agent with skills.
  • Testing Agent Changes

    How to verify an agent's changes with characterization tests and test-driven development (TDD), and which testing pitfalls to look out for.
  • Git & Secrets

    How to use Git safely alongside a coding agent and keep API keys, credentials, and other secrets safe.
  • Context, Permissions & config.toml

    How to use the VS Code Codex extension, manage context, control what an agent can access and change, and configure it with config.toml.
  • MCP & shadcn

    How to connect agents to external tools with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), including shadcn.

entries.content:
Sending a 5 GB video file might seem simple. You select the file, click Upload, wait for the progress bar to finish, and share a link with someone. But there are several things happening in the background while the file is being uploaded.

The file has to travel across a network, reach a server, and be stored somewhere before another person can download it. The service also needs to make sure that the recipient can access the file without accessing the sender's account. If the internet connection drops halfway through the upload, it needs a way to continue without sending the entire file again.

File transfer services use HTTP requests, storage systems, databases, encryption, and background processes to manage these tasks. But how does a website actually handle a file that's several gigabytes in size? Does it upload everything in one request? Where does the file go after the upload finishes? And what happens when its download link expires?

In this article, we'll look at how file transfer services handle large uploads, store files, generate download links, and manage interrupted connections and expired transfers. Then, once you understand the theory behind how it all works, we'll also build a basic chunked file uploader using Node.js to see some of these processes in action.

What We'll Cover:

Why Email Attachments Fail: SMTP Wasn't Designed for Large Files

Before looking at dedicated file transfer services, it helps to understand why we can't just attach massive files to an email. Sending large files through email is fundamentally flawed because the underlying architecture was built for text, not high-resolution media.

SMTP and Attachment Size Limits

Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) handles the transmission of email messages across the internet. Because servers have limited bandwidth and storage, email providers impose strict attachment size limits, usually capping out around 25 MB. However, these limits apply to the encoded message size, not just the original file sitting on your hard drive.

The Base64 Problem

Email attachments are commonly encoded using MIME and Base64 formats. Base64 is necessary because it converts binary data into text-compatible characters that email servers can safely route. While this solves the transmission problem, it creates a massive efficiency issue: this encoding increases the data size by approximately 33%.

You can read the foundational specifications for this in RFC 2045, which defines MIME's Base64 transfer encoding. In practice, this means a 30 MB video file will require roughly 40 MB of space before additional message overhead is even calculated, guaranteeing it will bounce back from most email servers.

The Core Architecture: What Happens Behind a File Transfer Service?

To bypass the limitations of email, file transfer services use a specialized, decoupled architecture. Having built a few of these systems myself, I believe establishing a clear mental model of the five major components is crucial for understanding the flow of data.

The Client

The journey begins in the client, which is usually a web browser or a desktop application where the sender selects a file. Modern browsers use JavaScript's File API to access file metadata, read the raw contents and intelligently divide the file into smaller, manageable parts before any data hits the network.

The Upload Server

Once the client starts sending data, the upload server steps in. This server receives the upload requests, authenticates the user, validates incoming data and coordinates the entire upload process. It acts as the traffic cop, ensuring that chunks of data are arriving in the correct format.

The Storage Layer

Traditional application servers are terrible at holding massive files, so the storage layer handles the actual heavy lifting. Uploaded files are typically routed directly to object storage solutions. This allows the system to scale infinitely without crashing the primary upload servers.

The Metadata Database

While the physical file goes to object storage, the application needs a way to remember what that file is. The metadata database stores critical information, including the original filename, file size, content type, the specific object storage key, a unique transfer identifier and the exact expiration timestamp.

The Download Server

When someone opens a shared link, the download server takes over. It checks the database to verify permissions and expiration dates, and if everything is valid, it retrieves the stored object from the storage layer for delivery.

Chunked and Resumable Uploads: How Large Files Survive Bad Internet Connections

Transferring a 5 GB file in one continuous network request is a disaster waiting to happen. If a connection drops at 99%, a single-request architecture forces the user to start all over again.

Breaking a Large File Into Smaller Chunks

To solve this, modern clients divide large files into smaller parts, such as 10 MB chunks. Each chunk is uploaded to the server as an independent HTTP request. The server meticulously tracks which chunks have arrived. Some advanced systems even allow multiple chunks to upload simultaneously in parallel, drastically reducing the overall waiting time.

It's important to note that chunked uploads are an architectural pattern, which is entirely different from HTTP chunked transfer encoding (a mechanism for framing an HTTP message body).

What Happens When the Internet Disconnects?

Suppose 80% of a massive file has successfully uploaded when your Wi-Fi randomly disconnects. Without resumable uploads, that progress is lost. With resumable architecture, the client reconnects and asks the server for the upload offset, the exact number of bytes successfully received and stored. The client then seamlessly continues uploading from that exact position.

Checksums: Making Sure Nothing Gets Corrupted

Network transfers can sometimes flip bits, resulting in corrupted files. To prevent this, clients generate a cryptographic hash (checksum) for an individual chunk before sending it. The server receives the chunk, calculates its own hash, and compares the two. If the checksums don't match, the server rejects the chunk and asks the client to try again.

If you're looking to implement this, the TUS Resumable Upload Protocol is a fantastic, standardized reference for managing upload offsets and checksum verification. Also, the Amazon S3 Multipart Upload Documentation provides an industry-standard blueprint for handling parallel transfers and retrying failed parts.

Storage and Link Generation: Where Does Your File Actually Go?

Once every chunk is verified and reassembled, the service needs a secure place to keep the file until the recipient is ready to download it.

Why Services Use Object Storage

In my opinion, attempting to store gigabytes of user uploads on a traditional local server directory is architectural malpractice. Instead, services rely on object storage. Files are stored as flat objects and each object is assigned a unique key. Object storage is highly durable and scales quite easily to accommodate millions of massive files simultaneously.

How a Download Link Is Created

The relationship between the stored file and its shareable link relies on the metadata database. When the upload finishes, the application saves the file's storage key in the database and generates a unique access token. The recipient receives a URL containing that specific token. When they click the link, the server reads the token, locates the relevant file in the database and checks the download permissions.

Why Are These Links Difficult to Guess?

A secure file transfer link relies heavily on high entropy, which is randomness that makes tokens mathematically near-impossible to predict. Also, secure systems use signed URLs. These are URLs containing cryptographic signatures that authorize access for a limited, strictly-enforced period.

As outlined in the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, a random link isn't automatically secure without appropriate access controls, expiration policies, and protection against token leakage.

Expiry and Cleanup: What Happens When a Transfer Expires?

File transfer services process petabytes of data, meaning they can't store uploaded files forever without going bankrupt. They rely on aggressive lifecycle management.

Time to Live (TTL)

Every transfer is assigned a Time to Live (TTL) or expiration timestamp. Once that time passes, the database instantly invalidates the transfer identifier, ensuring that the download link no longer authorizes access.

Automated Cleanup Jobs

Because link expiration and physical deletion aren't necessarily simultaneous, background workers or scheduled cron jobs handle the actual cleanup. These workers periodically scan the database to find expired transfers, mark them as permanently unavailable, delete the associated multi-gigabyte objects from the storage layer, and finally remove the outdated metadata.

Download Limits

Some services also allow senders to limit how many times a file can be downloaded. Once the download count reaches the threshold, the link behaves exactly as if the TTL had expired, offering an excellent way to control unauthorized distribution.

Security Layers: Protecting Files During Transfer and Storage

Security in file transfers is never about a single magic feature. It requires multiple layers of defense to keep data safe from interception or theft.

TLS Encryption in Transit

When data travels between the sender, the transfer service, and the recipient, it's heavily encrypted. Modern platforms use HTTPS backed by strict TLS protocols to ensure no one can snoop on the data packets mid-route.

For a deep dive into how this is configured at an enterprise level, NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 offers exhaustive guidelines for TLS implementations.

Encryption at Rest

Once the file arrives at the storage layer, encryption at rest ensures that even if a bad actor physically accessed the server hardware, they would only find scrambled, unreadable data. It's important to note that encryption at rest isn't the same as end to end encryption. The service provider still manages the encryption keys in a standard setup.

Password-Protected Links

To prevent unauthorized users from accessing a valid URL, senders can add a password. This creates a secondary access-control layer that must be cleared before the server will even attempt to fetch the file from object storage. Additional safeguards, like rate-limiting against automated password guessing, ensure this layer remains effective.

Real-World Examples: How Popular File Transfer Services Handle File Sharing

Seeing how established companies implement these concepts helps bridge the gap between theory and practice.

WeTransfer: Temporary Transfers and Password Protection

WeTransfer is built entirely around temporary shareable links. Transfers have strict expiration timelines and premium users can enforce password protection. According to their security documentation, they utilize standard TLS encryption during transit and AES-256 encryption at rest to secure files on their servers.

Dropbox Transfer: Sending Files Without Collaboration

Unlike a standard shared folder, Dropbox Transfer creates standalone downloadable links. Recipients don't need a Dropbox account to download the payload. They utilize configurable expiration dates, passwords, and automated download notifications, with maximum file size limits dictated by the sender's specific subscription plan.

Send Anywhere: Direct Transfers and Temporary Links

Send Anywhere takes a fascinating hybrid approach. Its six-digit key transfer mechanism operates in real-time for one-time use within a 10-minute window, often leveraging peer to peer connections. Conversely, its standard Share Link option falls back to a server-based architecture, uploading files and keeping the link valid for up to 48 hours.

Filemail: Large Transfers and Expiration Controls

Offering robust email and shareable-link delivery options, Filemail handles massive payloads easily. They provide highly configurable expiration controls and rigorous password protection. Their free service tier currently allows a 5 GB transfer limit, holding the data securely for a maximum seven-day storage period before automated cleanup takes over.

Hands-On: Build a Minimal Chunked File Uploader Using Node.js

Understanding the theory is great, but building it yourself proves how it actually works. Let's create a simple application that divides a file into smaller chunks in the browser, uploads them to a Node.js server and stitches them back together.

Step 1: Set Up the Node.js Project

You'll need Node.js, the Express framework, and multer for handling incoming file chunks. The built-in fs module will handle our file operations. First, create a Node project and install the required dependencies:

mkdir file-transfer
cd file-transfer
npm init -y
npm install express multer

Step 2: Divide the File Into Smaller Chunks

First, create a 

public
directory inside your project folder if it doesn't already exist. Then, create a file named 
upload.js
inside that directory. We'll use the browser's JavaScript File API and its 
slice()
method to read smaller portions of a file without loading the entire 5 GB payload into your computer's RAM.
const chunkSize = 5 * 1024 * 1024;

async function uploadFile(file) {
    const totalChunks = Math.ceil(file.size / chunkSize);
    const uploadId = crypto.randomUUID();

    for (let index = 0; index < totalChunks; index++) {
        const chunk = file.slice(
            index * chunkSize,
            (index + 1) * chunkSize
        );

        const formData = new FormData();
        formData.append("chunk", chunk);

        const response = await fetch(
            `/upload/${uploadId}/${index}/${totalChunks}`,
            {
                method: "POST",
                body: formData
            }
        );

        if (!response.ok) {
            throw new Error(`Chunk ${index} failed to upload`);
        }
    }

    const response = await fetch(`/complete/${uploadId}`, {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            totalChunks,
            filename: file.name
        })
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error("File reassembly failed");
    }
}

Here, 

crypto.randomUUID()
generates a unique ID for the upload. The browser sends each chunk separately and uses the same ID to associate all the chunks with the original file.

Step 3: Create an Upload Endpoint in Express

On the server side (

server.js
), we need an endpoint to receive and temporarily store each chunk. The server uses the upload ID and chunk index to determine where each part belongs, while the total number of chunks helps validate the upload. We use multer to parse the incoming multipart form data.
const express = require("express");
const multer = require("multer");
const fs = require("fs");
const path = require("path");
const { pipeline } = require("stream/promises");

const app = express();

app.use(express.static(path.join(__dirname, "public")));

const chunksDir = path.join(__dirname, "chunks");
const tempDir = path.join(chunksDir, "temp");

fs.mkdirSync(tempDir, { recursive: true });

const upload = multer({
    dest: tempDir,
    limits: { fileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024 }
});

app.post(
    "/upload/:id/:index/:total",
    upload.single("chunk"),
    async (req, res) => {
        try {
            const { id, index, total } = req.params;

            if (!req.file) {
                return res.status(400).send("No chunk received");
            }

            if (
                !/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/i.test(id) ||
                !Number.isInteger(Number(index)) ||
                !Number.isInteger(Number(total)) ||
                Number(total) < 1 ||
                Number(total) > 10000 ||
                Number(index) < 0 ||
                Number(index) >= Number(total)
            ) {
                return res.status(400).send("Invalid upload details");
            }

            const folder = path.join(chunksDir, id);

            await fs.promises.mkdir(folder, {
                recursive: true
            });

            await fs.promises.rename(
                req.file.path,
                path.join(folder, `${index}.part`)
            );

            res.send("Chunk received");

        } catch (error) {
            res.status(500).send("Upload failed");
        }
    }
);

The server stores each chunk using its upload ID and index, making it possible to identify and retrieve the individual parts when the upload is complete.

Step 4: Reassemble the Original File

Once the client confirms all chunks have been transmitted, it triggers a final reassembly route. The server first checks whether every expected chunk exists in the 

chunks/
directory. It then reads the chunks sequentially using 
fs.createReadStream()
and writes them to the same output file using 
fs.createWriteStream()
. The first chunk creates the file, while subsequent chunks are appended to it. Once the original file has been reassembled, the server deletes the temporary chunks to free up space.
const uploadsDir = path.join(__dirname, "uploads");

fs.mkdirSync(uploadsDir, { recursive: true });

app.use(express.json());

app.post("/complete/:id", async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { id } = req.params;
        const { totalChunks, filename } = req.body;

        if (
            !/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/i.test(id) ||
            !Number.isInteger(totalChunks) ||
            totalChunks < 1 ||
            totalChunks > 10000 ||
            typeof filename !== "string"
        ) {
            return res.status(400).send("Invalid upload details");
        }

        const folder = path.join(chunksDir, id);

        for (let i = 0; i < totalChunks; i++) {
            const chunkPath = path.join(folder, `${i}.part`);

            if (!fs.existsSync(chunkPath)) {
                return res.status(400).send(`Missing chunk ${i}`);
            }
        }

        const safeName =
            path.basename(filename).replace(/[^\w.-]/g, "_") ||
            "upload.bin";

        const outputPath = path.join(
            uploadsDir,
            `${id}-${safeName}`
        );

        await fs.promises.rm(outputPath, { force: true });

        for (let i = 0; i < totalChunks; i++) {
            const chunkPath = path.join(folder, `${i}.part`);

            await pipeline(
                fs.createReadStream(chunkPath),
                fs.createWriteStream(outputPath, {
                    flags: i === 0 ? "w" : "a"
                })
            );
        }

        await fs.promises.rm(folder, {
            recursive: true,
            force: true
        });

        res.json({
            message: "File assembled successfully"
        });

    } catch (error) {
        res.status(500).send("Reassembly failed");
    }
});

Finally, add the following code at the bottom of 

server.js
to start the Express server:
app.listen(3000, () => {
    console.log("Server running at http://localhost:3000");
});

Step 5: Test the Upload

Start the server by running 

node server.js
in your terminal. Then, open 
http://localhost:3000
 in your browser and select a medium-sized video file to test the upload. Open your browser's Network tab to observe how the file is divided into chunks and sent sequentially. Finally, check your server's 
uploads/
directory. The assembled file should have the same byte size as the original and should open correctly.

Create 

public/index.html
:



    File Uploader


    
Upload a File

Note: This implementation demonstrates the basic mechanics of chunked uploads and file reassembly. It doesn't implement resumable uploads, checksum verification, authentication, object storage, or temporary download links.

A production-grade file transfer service would also require persistent upload states, access controls, retry handling, integrity checks, and automated cleanup.

Conclusion: A Simple Link Hides a Lot of Engineering

Sending a large file involves several processes working together. From upload handling and chunk management in the browser to object storage, metadata tracking, encryption, and automated cleanup, each component has a specific role in making file transfers work.

These processes also explain how services handle interrupted uploads, control access to shared files, and remove data when a transfer expires. Understanding how these components work together makes it easier to see what happens behind the scenes whenever someone uploads a large file and shares a download link.
